title: Klausur Practice: Working Lives in the Age of AI
topic: Artificial intelligence and the future of work
general_instructions: Answer all three tasks in English. Refer to the text using line numbers where appropriate.

sources.title: The Quiet Desk
sources.label: Fictional practice text written for this exam. It is not a real publication and has no real author.
sources.text:
Every morning at half past eight, the office I work in grows a little quieter.
It is not that fewer people come in; it is that fewer of them need to talk.
The questions we once shouted across the room – Where is the latest version?
Who has the client's number? – are now answered instantly by software that
never sighs, never forgets and never asks for a pay rise.

Many of my colleagues welcome this. They describe the new tools as "a second
pair of hands" and point out, quite rightly, that nobody misses copying figures
from one spreadsheet into another. Yet I cannot shake the feeling that something
valuable is disappearing along with the drudgery.

Economists like to reassure us that technology has always created more jobs than
it destroyed. That may be true in the long run, but, as one of my younger
colleagues put it, "nobody lives in the long run." A graduate who cannot find an
entry-level position today will not be comforted by statistics about 2040.

What worries me most is not unemployment but apprenticeship. Junior staff used to
learn by doing the dull tasks that machines now perform. If the first rung of the
ladder is removed, how is anyone supposed to climb?

None of this means we should smash the machines. It means we should decide
deliberately which skills we want people to keep, and design work around them.
Companies that treat AI merely as a way to cut costs may save money this year;
those that use it to make their staff more capable will still have experienced
staff in ten years' time.

The quiet in our office is efficient. Whether it is also healthy depends on
choices we have barely begun to make.

tasks.instruction: Summarise the author's concerns about the growing use of artificial intelligence at work, as presented in the text.
Analyse how the author makes their warning persuasive. Consider the structure of the text and the use of language.
"Companies that treat AI merely as a way to cut costs may save money this year" (l. 19). Comment on this view.

marking.label: AI-generated practice scheme, not your teacher's

criteria.criterion: Main concerns covered in own words, simple present, no quotations, within word limit
Devices and structural moves are identified AND linked to their persuasive effect, with line references
Clear position, developed arguments with examples, a genuine counterargument, conclusion

expected_content: Office work is changing: software answers routine questions, so colleagues talk less
Author concedes that colleagues welcome relief from tedious tasks
Doubts economists' long-term reassurance: graduates need jobs now
Main worry: loss of learning opportunities for junior staff
Calls for deliberate decisions about which skills to keep; cost-cutting alone is short-sighted
Concession ('quite rightly') before 'Yet' makes the author seem balanced
Quotation of a younger colleague contrasts statistics with individual experience
Ladder metaphor plus rhetorical question makes the abstract problem concrete
Frame: return to the quiet office; antithesis 'efficient' vs 'healthy'
acceptable_alternatives: Focus on tone (calm, reflective) as a persuasive strategy
common_pitfalls: evaluating whether the author is right

expected_content: Arguments for long-term investment in staff (skills, motivation, succession)
A developed counterargument (e.g. small firms' margins, competition)
